text: Lesson 1 showed you a finished trace tree. This lesson is about how that tree actually gets built, hop by hop, as a real request moves through a system you already know how to deploy — a Kubernetes Ingress routing to a checkout Service, which calls an inventory Service, which queries a Postgres database.

A span is created the moment a unit of work starts and closed the moment it finishes — a timed region wrapped around real code, not a log written after the fact. A trace is the set of all spans sharing one trace ID, reassembled by their parent and child relationships into a tree. The gateway's span is the root, checkout's span is its child, the call to inventory is a child of that, and the Postgres query is a child of the inventory span.

Here's the mechanical problem: checkout-service and inventory-service are separate processes on separate pods that don't share memory. For inventory's span to attach as a child of checkout's span, checkout has to hand inventory the trace ID and its own span ID across the network — by injecting a header like this traceparent value into the outgoing request. Drop that header anywhere along the chain, at a proxy or a queue that doesn't forward metadata, and the trace doesn't error loudly. It just silently splits into two disconnected traces.

OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard most tracing tooling is built on. A Tracer creates spans; a Span carries a name, timing, and attributes like item SKU or rows returned; the Context carries the active trace and span ID through your code and across that network boundary; an Exporter ships finished spans out to a backend like Jaeger or Tempo for storage and querying. This code creates one span, attaches attributes, and closes it automatically.

At real traffic volumes, exporting a full trace for every single request is often more data than it's worth storing. Sampling decides which traces get kept — a common approach always keeps traces with an error or high latency, plus a small random slice of everything else. Set that rate too low, and the one trace you needed for an obscure, intermittent bug simply wasn't captured. It's a direct trade-off between storage cost and future coverage.

Spans get created, context propagates them across every hop, and sampling decides what survives — that's distributed tracing end to end. Next lesson turns that same judgment outward: deciding what's actually worth instrumenting at all, before you drown in signal nobody needed.
